summary: Kwangsoo Park is a scholar in Buddhist and religious studies. He earned an MA at the University of Iowa and a PhD at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, later serving as a professor at Wonkwang University (attested 2020).

Kyo Kano is a scholar of Indology and philosophy who studied at Keio University, Kyoto University, and the University of Vienna. Kano served as an assistant at Kyoto University (attested 1989) and associate professor at Kobe Women's University (attested 2000).

Kyojun Shimizutani (1891–1979) was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Keijun Shimizutani and at Tendai Sect University and Taisho University. He served as professor at Tendai Sect University (1919) and Taisho University (1926–1945), and head abbot at Senso-ji (~1952–1979).

Kyoko Amano is a scholar of Indology and linguistics who earned an MPhil at Osaka University and a doctorate at the University of Freiburg. She held research and teaching posts at Osaka University and Kyoto University (2013–2024).

Kyoko Fujii is a Buddhist studies and Indology scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo. She held professorships at Yokohama City, Hamamatsu, Hokkaido, and the International College for Postgraduate Buddhist Studies, and served as Director of the International Institute for Buddhist Studies.
Kyoko Tokuno is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Sinology. She held posts at the University of Oregon and the University of Washington, where she was attested as a professor in 2017.

Kyokuga Saeki (1828–1891) was a Buddhist studies and philosophy scholar who studied under numerous traditional teachers, including Gen'yū, Reiga, and Kasho Noyama. He served as the 143rd elder at Sennyu-ji from around 1888 to 1891.

Kyosho Hayashima (1914–1999) was an Indology and Buddhist studies scholar. He held academic posts as a lecturer at Yokohama City University (1962), assistant professor at Toyo University (1962), and professor at the University of Tokyo (1980).
Kyosho Tanaka is a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo. Around 1976, Tanaka served as an associate professor at Musashino University.
Kyoshun Todo (1916–2002) was a scholar of Buddhist studies. He taught at Bukkyo University, serving as an assistant professor (attested 1962) and later as a professor (attested 1988–1992).

Kyozo Yamada (1907–1989) worked in Buddhist and religious studies after studying at Tokyo Imperial University and under teachers such as Sogaku Harada. He worked at NOF Corporation (~1930–1967) and became the second head of Sanbo Zen in 1970.

Kyōtarō Nishikawa (1929–2023) was a scholar of history, archaeology, Japanology, and Buddhist studies who studied at Keio University. He served as Director-General of the Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties (~1990–1995) and at the Kanagawa Prefectural Museum (~1995–2012).

Károly Fiók (1857–1915) was an Indologist educated at Kölcsey Ferenc Teacher Training College, Berlin, Munich, and Eötvös Loránd University. He worked as a teacher at Budapest Reformed High School (1886–1907) and Debrecen Reformed College (1907–1915).
Käthe Marschner is an Indologist who studied at the University of Breslau, completing her PhD under the supervision of Otto Strauss around 1928–1933.

Käthe Neumann (1903–1989) was a scholar of religious studies, Indology, and Buddhist studies. After studying at Greifswald, Berlin, and Marburg under Johannes Nobel, she served as curator in charge of the Religionskundliche Sammlung from 1937 to 1968.
Kārlis Augusts Tennisons (1873–1962) was a Buddhist studies figure who studied at Saint Petersburg State University. He served as the director of Datsan Gunzechoinei from 1906 to 1923.
Kōgi Kudara (1945–2004) was a scholar of Buddhist studies, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He served as a professor at Ryukoku University from around 1978 to 2004.
Kōichi Kozaka is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Tibetology who studied under Hakuyu Hadano. Kozaka was attested as a professor at Osaka Kyoiku University in 1991.

Kōsen Imakita (1816–1892) studied under Kyokuso Hirose, Togai Fujisawa, Daisetsu Jōen, and Gisan Zenkai. Active in Buddhist studies and philosophy, he served as abbot at Eikō-ji (1858), doctrinal instructor in the Ministry of Religion (~1872–1875), and abbot of Engaku-ji (1875–1892).
Kōshō Ōtani (1911–2002) was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the First Higher School (~1929–1932) and Tokyo Imperial University (~1932–1935), and later succeeded Kozui Otani.
